note: Written to be spoken: one sentence or phrase per line; {"beat": s} is a deliberate pause; numbers and names are spelled the way they are said. `answer` plays after the learner answers a predict step.

lines: Tests tell you a change is right. They don't tell you how its cost grows when the data grows.
For that you need big O, big theta and big omega... and logarithms in any base.
The last of the five refreshers. All familiar? Swipe on to the memory hierarchy.
Big O is a ceiling. From some point on, the cost stays below some constant times the function.
Big omega is a floor. Big theta is both.
This job takes three n log n, plus eight n steps... where log is the number of halvings from n down to one.
Divide it by n log n. From two hundred and fifty six on, the answer stays between three and four.
So it's theta of n log n... and the constants, and the plus eight n, simply drop out.
Here's a trap.
You've just shown that job is theta of n log n.
A reviewer writes... it's big O of n squared.
Is that also true?
answer: Yes. Big O is only a ceiling, and n squared is a very high one... over a million times above the job, at a hundred million rows.
And it isn't a case, either. Best or worst, any cost can have a big O, a big omega and a big theta.
Say theta when you mean the growth rate.

lines: Now let the data grow.
At a thousand rows, nothing matters. Everything is instant.
At a hundred million orders, and a billion steps a second... n takes a tenth of a second. N log n, under three seconds.
And n squared? A hundred and sixteen days.
The bars are on a log scale... from microseconds, all the way up to a year.
Double the data, and n doubles... n log n grows a little more... and n squared quadruples.
A logarithm counts divisions.
How many times can you divide by the base before you reach one?
Bisect needed about ten tests for a thousand commits.
So how many halvings take a billion down to one?
answer: About thirty. Every ten halvings divide by about a thousand... and a billion is a thousand, times a thousand, times a thousand.
A million times more data than bisect's, for only twenty more halvings.

lines: Any base converts to any other.
Divide the natural log of x by the natural log of the base.
It's one length, measured with three rulers... base two, base ten, and base one thousand.
In your head, log base two is about three point three two times log base ten. So a billion, nine zeros, is about thirty halvings.
The bigger the base, the fewer the divisions.
A billion needs about thirty halvings, but only three divisions by a thousand... and just over two by sixteen thousand, three hundred eighty four.
Indexes and sorts divide by hundreds, or thousands, at a time... so their logarithms are tiny.
Here's the orders index.
A hundred million orders, with a Postgres B-tree on the order id.
One page holds about four hundred entries... and on an inner page, each entry points to a page below.
So every level multiplies the reach by about four hundred.
How many levels, from the root down to a leaf?
answer: Four. Three levels of four hundred reach only sixty four million keys.
The fourth reaches over twenty five billion.
Any fan-out from a hundred to four hundred and sixty four gives four levels. A binary tree would need twenty seven.

lines: Sorting is the same logarithm, with a big base.
The nightly job sorts about a trillion bytes, and memory holds sixteen thousand, three hundred and eighty four blocks.
One pass makes sixty four sorted runs.
The merge takes up to sixteen thousand at once, one block for each run and one for the output, so one more pass merges all sixty four.
Two passes, and each one reads and writes all those bytes. Merge two at a time, and it's seven.
Big O throws away constants on purpose.
So it can't tell you seconds.
Two scans of the same hundred million rows... same count, same growth... can take very different times, depending on where the data lives.
In the cache, a hundred million steps take a tenth of a second. If every step waits on a disk, it's hours.
So... five things to keep.
Big O is a ceiling, omega a floor, theta both. A logarithm counts divisions. Any base converts with a natural log.
A big base makes a tiny log: four levels, two passes.
And big O counts steps, not seconds.
Next up... the memory hierarchy, where one step can cost a nanosecond, or tens of milliseconds.
